title: Associate Exam
description: 40 questions per attempt from a pool of 50, covering data sources, bands and groups, calculations, parameters, sub-reports and publishing. Pass mark is 80%. Open-book — browse any page, hover glossary terms, or ask the AI assistant. Your answers are saved as you go. Explanations appear after submission.

questions.scenario: An invoice must match a printed template exactly with fixed positions for the logo and address block, a header on every page, and subtotals per customer. Business users will run the report once it is published.
questions.prompt: Which tool should the invoice be authored in?
options: Interactive Reports
Report Designer
Dashboard Designer
Analyzer
questions.explanation: **Report Designer** lays out banded, pixel-positioned content with page headers and per-group subtotals, which is the control a fixed print template needs, and it publishes the report for business users to run.
questions.source: Getting Started with Pentaho Business Analytics

questions.scenario: A colleague sends a `.prpt` file to a team member who has Report Designer installed but lacks a network route to the database the report queries.
questions.prompt: What happens when they attempt to preview the report?
options: It will not open at all unless its data source is reachable
It opens, but the query fails, as the file holds no rows
It renders the layout with placeholder values instead
It renders from rows the file cached at its last run
questions.explanation:
A `.prpt` file is a **definition file** containing the layout, query, and connection details, but it does not contain the underlying data. Because it is only a definition, the file can be opened without a connection, but the preview will fail because the **query** cannot reach the database.

Report Designer does not cache rows; therefore, there are no values to render if the query fails.
questions.source: Getting Started with Pentaho Business Analytics

questions.scenario: An author installs Pentaho on a new laptop and runs `start-pentaho.bat` to bring up the Pentaho Server. The console window opens and closes again at once, and the sign-in page never loads.
questions.prompt: What should the author check first?
options: That the sample database is running before the server
That Report Designer is open before the server starts
That JAVA_HOME is set and points at the right JDK
That the SampleData connection holds its user and password
questions.explanation: A Pentaho Server console window that closes immediately almost always comes down to the **Java home setting**: `JAVA_HOME` is unset or points at the wrong JDK. Check it with `echo $env:JAVA_HOME`, and see `set-pentaho-env.bat`, in the same folder as `start-pentaho.bat`, for what the server expects.

questions.scenario: Report Designer starts normally, but every sample report on the Welcome screen fails to render. A colleague with an identical installation can view them without issue.
questions.prompt: What is the most likely explanation?
options: The samples must be published once before they display.
The Welcome screen renders them from a cache built at first login.
The installation has no license, so it renders no reports.
The sample database is not running, so the data source fails.
questions.explanation: The sample reports are linked to the **sample database** that runs alongside the server. If this database is not running, the report fails to render because it cannot connect to its data source.

questions.scenario: A report appears correctly formatted on the design canvas with all elements positioned as intended.
questions.prompt: What does Preview show that the canvas cannot?
options: The style sheet, which the canvas deliberately leaves out
Publishing errors, found by checking against the repository
The same layout at print resolution, and nothing more
Real rows: where groups break, how many rows, and where pages end
questions.explanation: The **Preview** feature runs the query and the reporting engine over real data, which allows the system to calculate and display accurate **group breaks**, row counts, and page overflows. In contrast, the canvas only displays a single representative band of data.

questions.scenario: An author must show the No Data band on the design canvas so a message can be added to it. In the same report, the quantity number field needs a pale background color.
questions.prompt: Where are these two settings made?
options: Style pane for both the band and the color
Attributes pane for the band, Style pane for the color
Style pane for the band, Attributes pane for the color
Attributes pane for both the band and the color
questions.explanation:
The **Style pane** holds an element's visual and positional options, so the background color is set there, in the `bg-color` property under text.

The **Attributes pane** holds the low-level properties and the input and output options, including `hide-on-canvas`. A band such as No Data is shown on the canvas by selecting it in the Structure pane and setting its `hide-on-canvas` attribute to `false`.

questions.scenario: A report holds only a bar chart in its Report Header, showing total sales for each product line by year. Its query returns every order line, about 3,000 rows, and the totals are worked out as the report runs. The author wants the report to do less work.
questions.prompt: Where should the totals be calculated?
options: In the Report Footer, where every row has already been read
In a Sum function in the Data pane that feeds the chart
In the query, with a SUM grouped by product line and year
In a sub-report that runs its own copy of the query
questions.explanation:
With `SUM` and `GROUP BY` in the query, the database does the aggregation and the chart receives one row per product line and year instead of every order line. The engine could total the detail rows itself, but a few aggregated rows are far cheaper to ship than thousands, so the rule is to **aggregate in SQL** wherever possible.

The chart's **data collector** builds its dataset from whatever rows the query returns, during the engine's first pass, so the chart in the Report Header shows the same totals from far fewer rows.

questions.scenario: A report must read order data directly from the company's PostgreSQL warehouse using SQL written by the report author.
questions.prompt: Which data source type should the report use?
options: Pentaho Analysis
Metadata
XML
JDBC
questions.explanation: A **JDBC** data source provides a way to connect to a relational database and execute custom SQL statements directly against the source tables.

questions.scenario: Report writers do not know the database schema, but they must produce reports where specific column formatting and access rules are applied consistently across all reports.
questions.prompt: Why should these reports point to a metadata model instead of a direct JDBC connection?
options: The model caches query results, so it runs faster than raw JDBC.
The model translates the SQL into each writer's own dialect.
A JDBC connection cannot be shared by more than one report.
Names, formatting, and security are set once, above the schema.
questions.explanation: A **metadata model** is a layer above the physical database schema. Business names, formatting, and security rules are defined in it once, so writers never see raw tables and every report built on the model inherits the rules.

questions.scenario: An element in the Details band appears once for every row returned, while the same element moved into a Group Header appears only once per group.
questions.prompt: What does this behavior indicate about how bands function?
options: A band prints once per thing it stands for, so placement sets repetition.
The group header hides duplicates but still renders the element per row.
Bands set vertical position only; a property on each element sets repetition.
Each element renders once wherever it sits; only the Details band loops.
questions.explanation:
The **band type** determines the repetition logic for any element placed within it. Because a band is printed once for every unit it represents—such as a row or a group—the placement of an element determines its output frequency.

Repetition is not an individual property of an element; instead, the element follows the behavior of the **container band** in which it resides.
questions.source: Adding Report Elements and Creating Groups

questions.scenario: A flat list of order lines must be broken into sections where each product line has its own heading and subtotal.
questions.prompt: What does adding a group on `PRODUCTLINE` do?
options: Runs a separate query for each product line in turn
Sorts the query's rows by product line without changing the layout
Splits the rows into sections with their own header and footer bands
Hides every product line except the one that is selected
questions.explanation:
Adding a **group** starts a new section every time the `PRODUCTLINE` value changes, with its own header and footer bands for labels and totals.

A group does not sort the rows: it relies on the query's `ORDER BY`, and it runs no extra query.
questions.source: Adding Report Elements and Creating Groups

questions.scenario: A report must highlight a specific inventory metric. The quantity in stock should appear in red text when it falls below 1,000 and in black otherwise.
questions.prompt: How is this achieved in Report Designer?
options: A setting chosen in the publish dialog
A group sorted on the quantity column
A formula on the element's text-color style property
A CASE expression in the SQL that returns the color
questions.explanation:
In Report Designer any **style property** can carry a formula, evaluated for each row. On the `text-color` property, this formula is the whole technique:

```
=IF([QUANTITYINSTOCK]<1000;"RED";"BLACK")
```

questions.scenario: A report grouped by product line needs each group's total Quantity in Stock beneath the group's detail rows.
questions.prompt: What should the author add?
options: A Sum function reset on the group, placed in the group footer
A sub-report in the Details band that adds the rows up
A parameter whose default value is the group's total
A second query that sums the quantity for each product line
questions.explanation: A **Sum function** added in the Data pane with the **Reset on Group Name** property set to the product-line group calculates the total for each group. Placing this function in the group footer ensures it prints immediately after the detail rows of that group.

questions.scenario: A multi-page report must display the company name and the current run date at the top of every page instead of only on the first page.
questions.prompt: Which band should hold these fields?
options: Report Footer
Page Header
Group Header
Report Header
questions.explanation:
The **Page Header** band prints at the top of every page in the report.

This ensures that consistent information, such as a company name, is repeated on every page for the reader.

questions.scenario: A report uses a region parameter. Users frequently mistype region names, which results in empty reports. The prompt must be configured to only offer valid regions.
questions.prompt: How should the parameter be set up?
options: Check the value with a formula once the report has finished running
Back it with a query listing the regions, shown as a drop-down
Give it a default value, which blocks any other value
Match region names in the main query case-insensitively
questions.explanation: Backing the parameter with a **query-based list** offers only the regions that exist, and with **strict values** set it rejects anything else, so the mistake cannot be made.

questions.scenario: An author adds a Territory parameter to a report. The prompt appears in preview, but selecting a specific territory still returns all records from every territory.
questions.prompt: What is missing?
options: A WHERE clause in the query that uses ${TERRITORY}
Publishing, since prompts only filter on the server
A default value, so the parameter applies on first run
A group on Territory, which the prompt then filters
questions.explanation: Defining a parameter only creates the **prompt**; it does not filter anything by itself. The selection takes effect only when the query references the parameter, as in `WHERE territory IN (${TERRITORY})`.

questions.scenario: Beside each customer, a report must list that customer's open invoices. The invoice rows come from a different query than the customer rows.
questions.prompt: Why does this call for a sub-report rather than a group?
options: A group can break on only one column, and this needs two.
A group only arranges rows already returned; a sub-report runs its own query.
A group cannot sit in the Details band, so side content must be a sub-report.
A sub-report runs its query once for the whole report, so it is faster.
questions.explanation:
A **group** only organizes the results of the primary query, whereas a **sub-report** executes its own independent query in the context of the parent row.

Because the invoice data is retrieved from a separate query, it requires the sub-report to fetch and display the secondary result set linked by a parameter.

questions.scenario: A bar chart displays sales by order status. Managers want to click a bar and open a published Order Status report that is filtered to the status of that bar.
questions.prompt: What does the chart need?
options: A url-formula using DRILLDOWN that passes the bar's category
A sub-report of the Order Status report placed inside the chart
A second value column carrying each status's orders
3-D rendering, so that each bar can take a click
questions.explanation:
The chart needs a **url-formula** that uses the **DRILLDOWN** function. It is evaluated for each bar and builds the viewer URL for the target report, passing the bar's category as its status parameter.

Only HTML output makes the bars clickable.

questions.scenario: A report must be distributed to 30 business users. A colleague suggests emailing the `.prpt` file to each user to avoid server dependency and allow them to keep personal copies.
questions.prompt: How should that proposal be judged?
options: Accept it for now, since publishing later keeps the copies in step.
Reject it, because .prpt files cannot be sent by email at all.
Reject it: each user needs the tool and data access, and copies drift.
Accept it: a .prpt carries its own data, so only the file size matters.
questions.explanation:
A `.prpt` file is a **report definition** and does not contain any data. To view the report, a user must have access to the required tools and a **reachable database**, which is not guaranteed for all recipients.

Distributing individual files to 30 people causes the files to diverge from the original version over time. Publishing the report ensures a single, consistent copy is run against the central data on the server.

questions.scenario: A report is published to a repository. An author opens the local `.prpt` file, corrects a column heading, and saves the local file.
questions.prompt: Why do users still see the old heading?
options: Users must sign out and back in to see the saved change.
The server caches rendered output until a timer runs out.
Publishing uploaded a copy, so the fix must be published again.
Headings live in the repository's metadata and are edited there.
questions.explanation: Publishing creates a **separate copy** of the file in the repository, so updating the local file does not change the version on the server. The edited file must be published again for users to see the change.

questions.scenario: A summary report lists sales by region. A user wants to click a region to open a detail report showing only the transactions for that specific region.
questions.prompt: Which three components are required to implement this drill-through?
options: A hyperlink on the region element that targets the published detail report
The region value passed to the target report as a parameter
A matching parameter on the detail report, which its query uses
Both reports built from the same query, so the clicked row carries across
The detail report embedded as a sub-report inside the summary's region band
questions.explanation:
A drill-through needs a **hyperlink** on the element that opens the published detail report, and the region's value passed to that report as a **parameter**.

The detail report must have a **matching parameter** that its query uses to filter the results. Without it, the detail report opens unfiltered.

questions.scenario: A report is developed against a test database on a local machine and is later deployed to a server that must query a production database without modifying the report source.
questions.prompt: Which connection access type suits this requirement?
options: Native JDBC, with the production URL typed into the report
Native JDBC, with the credentials passed in a hidden parameter
JNDI, a named connection each environment resolves itself
ODBC, which the server translates into its own connection
questions.explanation:
A **JNDI connection** stores only a name rather than specific connection details. This allows the report to be deployed to different environments where the local system resolves the name to a test database and the server resolves the same name to a production database.

Because the resolution happens at the environment level, the credentials remain secured on the server and the report file does not need to be edited for different environments.

questions.scenario: A report grouped by Territory, then by Customer, shows the same territory header several times, scattered through the output, with no error.
questions.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
options: The query does not ORDER BY territory before customer
Report Designer caps each group at a fixed row count
The group was defined on the Details band instead
The Details Header is set to repeat on every page
questions.explanation:
The reporting engine determines when to start a new group based on whether the value of the group field changes from one record to the next. If the data is not sorted by the grouping field, the engine will trigger a new **group header** every time the value flips back and forth, resulting in repeated headers for the same territory.

To ensure headers appear only when a value actually changes, the underlying SQL query must include a specific `ORDER BY` clause to keep identical group values contiguous.

questions.scenario: A report gets its rows from a PDI transformation. The transformation needs a region and a start date as parameters, and report users must choose both values each time they run it.
questions.prompt: How should the users' values reach the transformation?
options: As environment variables the server sets for each user's session
As report parameters, each mapped to a transformation parameter
As a WHERE clause on the rows the transformation returns
As parameter defaults edited in the transformation before each run
questions.explanation:
A **Pentaho Data Integration** data source runs a `.ktr` transformation and uses the rows of the step selected in the data source as its data set. Its Edit Parameter dialog maps each of the transformation's **named parameters** to a report parameter, so the values users choose in the prompts are passed into the transformation when the report runs.

The report parameters themselves are added in the Data tab, by right-clicking Parameters and choosing Add Parameter.

questions.scenario: A report reads an XML file in which every order is an `order` element inside a single `document` element. Previewing the XML data source returns one record instead of one record for each order.
questions.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
options: An XML data source returns one record for each file
The XPath query selects the document element, not each order
The query has no ORDER BY to split the orders apart
The orders need a group before they become records
questions.explanation:
XML is a tree with several levels, not a flat table of rows and columns, so an XML data source needs an **XPath query** to identify which nodes of the document count as **records**. Each node the expression selects becomes one record.

An expression that selects the `document` element finds a single node and so returns one record. The expression `/document/order` selects every `order` node inside it, which gives one record per order.

questions.scenario: Each product line group header must display a dynamic label such as Product Line: Classic Cars, where the specific name changes for every group.
questions.prompt: Which single element displays this dynamic content?
options: A message field reading Product Line: $(PRODUCTLINE)
A label whose text is the word PRODUCTLINE
A label with the words Product Line: typed into it
A number field bound to the report's PRODUCTLINE column
questions.explanation:
A **message field** acts as a template that replaces the `$(PRODUCTLINE)` variable with the current value every time the band prints.

This allows a single element to generate unique text for each group by dynamically injecting the value from the underlying data source.
questions.source: Adding Report Elements and Creating Groups

questions.scenario: A designer attempts to move a text field from the Details band to the Group Header band in a report template, but the field stays in its original band and the band expands in height.
questions.prompt: How is the element moved into the Group Header?
options: Hold Ctrl while dragging it across the band border
Change its band setting in the element's Attributes pane
Delete the Details band so the element moves up
Cut it from Details and paste it into the Group Header
questions.explanation:
Because elements cannot be moved between bands by dragging, the item must be **cut and pasted** to change its band assignment.

Dragging an element toward a border will only resize the band rather than moving the element across the boundary.
questions.source: Adding Report Elements and Creating Groups

questions.scenario: A product report grouped by product line is exported to Excel for the sales team. The team wants each product line on its own worksheet.
questions.prompt: What should the author set?
options: `pagebreak-after` set to true on the group
`repeat-header` set to true on the Group Header
`avoid-page-break` set to true on the group
`display-on-first-page` set to true on the Group Header
questions.explanation:
Setting `pagebreak-after` to true on the group tells the **pagination pass** to end the page once that group's footer has printed. The Excel exporter has no pages, so it maps each **page break** to a new worksheet, and each product line arrives on its own tab.

This follows a general rule: the engine produces one laid-out result, and each **output processor** renders it the way its format can. PDF and print honor the same page break literally.

questions.scenario: A product listing looks correct in the Preview window. Its HTML and Excel exports, however, show unusual layout problems in the Details band.
questions.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
options: The grid and guides were saved into the exported files.
Dragged fields store no exact position, so exports guess one.
The query does not sort the rows by the group field.
Elements in the Details band overlap one another.
questions.explanation:
Report Designer places every element at an absolute position in its band, and elements do not flow around each other. **Overlapping elements** may look agreeable in the Preview window and in some kinds of output, but the HTML and Excel output formats have unusual problems with them, so the guidance is to avoid overlapping elements altogether.

Each **output processor** renders the same laid-out result the way its own format can.

questions.scenario: A group's total must appear in the Group Header, above the group's rows. An ItemSumFunction placed there shows too small a number.
questions.prompt: What should be used instead?
options: A formula in the header that multiplies the first row by the row count
An ItemSumFunction with Reset on Group Name left blank
A TotalGroupSumFunction, which has each group's total from pass one
A second query that sums each group, run for every header
questions.explanation:
A **TotalGroupSumFunction** calculates the total for each group during an initial pass of the data. This allows the engine to provide the complete total for the group even when that value is required in the header before the group rows are processed.

In contrast, an ItemSumFunction is a running sum that is only accurate once the final row of a group has passed.

questions.scenario: In an order report, the `STATUS` cell must have a red background for both `Cancelled` and `Disputed` orders, and a green background for every other status.
questions.prompt: Which formula belongs on the cell's `bg-color` property?
options: `=IF(AND([STATUS]="Cancelled";[STATUS]="Disputed");"red";"green")`
`=IF(OR(STATUS="Cancelled";STATUS="Disputed");"red";"green")`
`=IF(OR([STATUS]="Cancelled";[STATUS]="Disputed");red;green)`
`=IF(OR([STATUS]="Cancelled";[STATUS]="Disputed");"red";"green")`
questions.explanation:
Report Designer formulas follow **OpenFormula** syntax: column names in uppercase inside square brackets, such as `[STATUS]`, and values in quotes, including color values such as `"red"`. The **OR** function returns true when either comparison is true, so the `IF` returns `"red"` for a `Cancelled` order and for a `Disputed` one, and `"green"` for every other status.

Placed on the element's `bg-color` style property, the formula drives **conditional formatting**: it is evaluated for each row, and the color it returns paints the cell's background.

questions.scenario: A long inventory listing has many narrow columns, and readers lose track of which values belong to the same row. The manager wants every other detail row shaded.
questions.prompt: What should the author add?
options: A bottom border on the Details band
A Row Banding function
A Hide Repeating function
One background color set on the Details band
questions.explanation:
The **Row Banding** function alternates the background color of each item band in a group, so every other detail row prints shaded. It belongs to the **Report functions**, the category of functions that modify the layout of the rendered report.

Like other functions, it is added from the Data pane by right-clicking Functions and choosing Add Functions.

questions.scenario: An author writes a formula that divides `[QUANTITYINSTOCK]` by `[RunningStock]`, a running Sum function in the report. The Formula Editor shows no warning, but it also shows no result for the formula.
questions.prompt: Why does the editor show no result?
options: The function's value is calculated only while the report runs.
The formula contains an error that the editor does not report.
Formulas cannot divide, so the division belongs in the query.
A formula can refer to query columns, but never to functions.
questions.explanation:
The Formula Editor warns when the formula text contains an error; otherwise it tries to show the result by evaluating the formula against the first data row. A running total is a **stateful function**: it maintains its state during report generation, so its value is **calculated during the execution of the report** and there is nothing for the editor to show beforehand.

The missing result does not mean the formula is wrong. Functions, query columns, and parameters share one namespace, so a formula can refer to a function by name just as it refers to `[QUANTITYINSTOCK]`.

questions.scenario: A published report is accessed by users in different countries. The price column must display the appropriate currency symbol based on the locale of the user running the report.
questions.prompt: What should the format pattern use for the symbol?
options: A formula that picks $ or € from the user's name
Two price columns, one per country, chosen by a parameter
$, which each locale converts into its own currency
¤, which each locale replaces with its currency symbol
questions.explanation:
The format attribute is a **Java DecimalFormat** pattern. The use of the `¤` character ensures that the system replaces the symbol at run time with the specific currency symbol associated with the user's locale, such as `$` for the United States or `€` for Germany.

Using a literal `$` in the pattern would result in a dollar sign being displayed regardless of the locale.

questions.scenario: Forty reports share the company colors and fonts, and a rebrand is scheduled for next quarter.
questions.prompt: Which approach makes the rebrand cheapest?
options: The formatting toolbar, copying one report's styles across
One stylesheet (.prptstyle) linked by every report, changed once
Styles set on each report's master report, changed 40 times
A copy of the stylesheet embedded in each of the reports
questions.explanation: Using a **linked stylesheet** (.prptstyle) allows all reports to reference a single file for colors and fonts. This ensures that a rebrand requires only one edit to update all 40 reports.

questions.scenario: A 30-page sales report is printed and handed out page by page at a meeting. Each page must show, at the bottom, its own page number together with the total number of pages.
questions.prompt: Which function should the Page Footer field use?
options: The Total Page Count function
The Count by Page function
The Page of Pages function
The Page function
questions.explanation:
The **Page of Pages** function, in the Common category, prints the current page number against the total, such as 3 / 12. It is added from the Data pane and bound to a text field in the Page Footer through that field's `field` attribute.

The total is known only once the **pagination pass** has laid out the entire report, which is why page functions belong in the Page Header and Page Footer bands. Because the count is measured, it stays right when a parameter changes the length of the report.

questions.scenario: A designer changes the `text-color` of a Group Header band from blue to green. Most elements in the band turn green, but two labels stay blue.
questions.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
options: The two labels carry a color setting of their own.
Labels take their color from the Page Header, not their band.
A band's color reaches only elements added after the change.
The report's default style outranks the band for labels.
questions.explanation:
Every visual property is a **style key**, stored per element. A key that an element has not set is inherited from the band it sits in, then from the report's default style, much like CSS, so a new `text-color` on the band reaches every element that has no color of its own.

An element's own `text-color` **overrides** the inherited value, so those two labels keep theirs. The formatting toolbar writes the same keys as the Style pane, so a color applied to them from the toolbar is also a setting of their own.

questions.scenario: A promotional banner appears in the Report Header of 20 published reports. Marketing replaces the banner image each month in a repository folder that all 20 reports can reach on the server.
questions.prompt: Which way of adding the banner is best?
options: Link the image, so publishing copies it into each report.
Link the image, so each run fetches the current banner.
Embed the image, so the server refreshes it from the folder.
Embed the image, so each report carries its own copy.
questions.explanation:
A **linked image** keeps only its path, and the engine's resource loader fetches the file at run time, relative to the report's location; on the server that is a repository path. Every run of the 20 reports therefore shows the banner Marketing saved most recently, with no report edited or republished.

The rule is to embed anything the report cannot function without, and to link only what **changes independently of the report** and is guaranteed to exist where the report runs. The banner meets both conditions.

questions.scenario: A sub-report showing each customer's payment history is placed in the Details band of a report that lists 500 customers.
questions.prompt: How many times does the sub-report run?
options: Once for each customer row: 500 times
Once for each page of the master report
Once for each group in the master report
Once, before the master report starts
questions.explanation: The **sub-report** execution is determined by the band in which it is placed. Because the Details band is processed once for every record in the data set, the sub-report executes 500 times, once for each customer record.

questions.scenario: A chart in a Report Header correctly summarizes every detail row printed below it, even though the header is printed before those rows.
questions.prompt: How does the chart already have that data?
options: The chart runs its own copy of the report's query.
The chart shows figures cached from the previous run.
The engine's first pass collects every row before the header prints.
The header is printed last of all, then moved to the top of the page.
questions.explanation: The reporting engine performs two passes over the data. During the first pass, the **data collector** visits every row to build the dataset, and when the header prints in the second pass, the chart renders the collected information.

questions.scenario: A chart must show `SALES` for each year as bars and `VOLUME` for each year as a line. The line needs its own scale on the right of the chart.
questions.prompt: How should the chart be set up?
options: A Bar Line chart, with `VOLUME` on its Secondary DataSource tab
A Bar Line chart, with `VOLUME` added as a series-by-field
A Bar chart, with `SALES` and `VOLUME` both as value-columns
A Waterfall chart, with `VOLUME` as a second value column
questions.explanation:
A **Bar Line chart** takes two data sources, one for the bars and one for the line, set on its Primary DataSource and **Secondary DataSource** tabs. Here the primary has the year as its `category-column` and `SALES` in `value-columns`; the secondary has the same `category-column` with `VOLUME`, which draws the line.

The scale on the left is configured under Y-Axis and the scale on the right under **Y2-Axis**, so the line is read against its own scale.

questions.scenario: An author drags a Sub-report element into the Report Header, to the right of a chart, so a small table can print beside it. In preview, the table prints at the left edge of the page instead.
questions.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
options: Preview places every sub-report at the left edge until it is published
It was inserted as banded, which stacks at the parent's left edge
It was inserted as inline, which starts at the parent's left edge
It reuses the master's query, so it cannot sit beside the master's chart
questions.explanation:
An **inline sub-report** occupies a rectangle at the element's x and y position within the parent band, so it can print beside a chart. A **banded sub-report** stacks at the parent's left edge like another band, and a master report prints its sections from the left edge of the page (x=0), so that is where this table appears.

The choice is made in the Insert Subreport dialog; inserting the table as **Inline** keeps it beside the chart.

questions.scenario: A report that uses a native JDBC connection to MySQL previews successfully in Report Designer but fails in the User Console with a driver error after publication.
questions.prompt: What is the most likely fix?
options: Republish the report with its images embedded
Add the driver JAR to the report as a resource
Put the MySQL JDBC driver on the server as well
Run the report once in Report Designer after publishing
questions.explanation: The reporting engine on the server executes the report independently of the local workstation. Therefore, a **native JDBC connection** requires the appropriate driver to be installed on the server environment to function correctly.

questions.scenario: A manager wants to create a bookmark that opens a published report directly to the results for the EMEA region without navigating the User Console.
questions.prompt: Which option provides this functionality?
options: A User Console Favorite, which remembers the last parameter values
A copy of the .prpt saved with EMEA as its default
A schedule that runs the report for EMEA each morning
The report's /viewer URL, with the parameter in its query string
questions.explanation: Every published report generates a **viewer URL** derived from its repository path. By appending specific values as **query-string** arguments to this URL, a bookmark can be created that automatically loads the report with the intended parameters applied.

questions.scenario: A long report viewed as HTML opens with a list of its product lines. Readers want to click a product line in that list and jump to its section further down the same report.
questions.prompt: Which hyperlink option should the author use?
options: Self
URL
Manual Linking
Pentaho Repository
questions.explanation: Of the four hyperlink options in Report Designer, **Manual Linking** is the one for navigating inside a report: the link is configured by hand and moves within the report using **HTML anchors**. That lets each product line in the opening list link to its own section further down the same report.

questions.scenario: A summary report links each product code to a published detail report. The author plans to use the URL option and type in the test server's full viewer address, and both reports move to a production server next month.
questions.prompt: How should that plan be judged?
options: Accept it: publishing to production rewrites any server address in links.
Accept it: only a URL link can pass the product code to the detail report.
Reject it: a Pentaho Repository link targets whichever server runs the report.
Reject it: Self is the option that links to reports on the same server.
questions.explanation:
A link built with the **Pentaho Repository** option is saved as a `DRILLDOWN` formula in the element's `url` style, and its **server argument** is `NA()`, which means the server the report is running on. It carries each row's product code to the detail report as a parameter.

Once both reports are on production, the same link opens the detail report there with no edit, while a typed test-server address would keep pointing at the test server.

questions.scenario: Users select a product line and then select a country from a list. Users report that the country list contains options that do not have any associated orders for the chosen product line.
questions.prompt: What is the best fix?
options: Make the country list's query use the product-line parameter.
Merge both choices into one parameter listing every pair.
Validate the pair after the run and show a warning message.
Make the country prompt free text so any value can be typed.
questions.explanation: The **query for a list parameter** can reference another parameter. By making the country list query dependent on the product line parameter, the framework automatically refreshes the available choices whenever the first selection changes, creating a **cascading parameter** effect that ensures only valid options are displayed.

questions.scenario: A sales report has a Year parameter. Its prompt must open with the current year already selected while users can still pick any other year, and nobody should have to edit the report each January.
questions.prompt: How should the pre-selected year be supplied?
options: A Post-Processing Formula that replaces the chosen year
A Default Value holding this year, typed into the dialog
A Default Value Formula that computes the current year
A Display Value Formula that shows the current year
questions.explanation: In the Add Parameter dialog, a parameter's pre-selected value comes from either a **Default Value**, which is static, or a **Default Value Formula**, which computes it. A formula that works out the current year moves the prompt's starting choice on by itself each January, and because it only sets the default, users can still select any other year.

questions.scenario: A report's query filters with `WHERE productline IN (${product_var})`. A user picks a product line whose name contains an apostrophe, and the report returns the right rows.
questions.prompt: What keeps the apostrophe from breaking the SQL?
options: The engine escapes each apostrophe, then splices the value in
The value is bound to a placeholder, not spliced into the SQL
Strict values clean the value before it reaches the query
The prompt strips punctuation from the value before the run
questions.explanation:
Before the query runs, the SQL data factory finds each `${name}` reference, replaces it with a JDBC `?` placeholder, and binds the parameter's value through a **prepared statement**. The value never becomes part of the SQL text, so an apostrophe in a product line name cannot break the query or inject anything.

The same **bind marker** is why `${product_var}` needs no quotes in the query.

questions.scenario: Managers want one report that lists either product lines or product vendors, chosen at run time. A colleague proposes adding a parameter to the query's WHERE clause to switch between the two columns.
questions.prompt: How should that proposal be judged?
options: Accept it, provided the parameter is Mandatory so a column is always chosen.
Accept it: a WHERE clause parameter can name the column the query returns.
Reject it: no parameter can change columns, so build two separate reports.
Reject it: a WHERE clause filters values; a query formula can pick columns.
questions.explanation:
**Simple parameterization** references the parameter, as `${NAME}`, in a `WHERE` clause; it constrains the values the query returns and cannot change its columns or structure. Letting readers choose among columns is **advanced parameterization**, which is expressed as a formula and executed along with the query.

In Report Designer that is a JDBC (Custom) data source with a **query formula** on the Master Report, such as `="SELECT DISTINCT " & [paramexample] & " AS COL1 FROM PRODUCTS"`, with the report field named after the `AS` alias. One report then serves both lists.
